A subgroup discovered in a trial is reported through the standard analysis the
trial would have run had that subgroup been the only one: the treatment
coefficient of the working model fitted within it, a Cox log hazard ratio here.
Selection by an effect-driven rule — rewarding large estimated effects subject
to screening and size criteria — inflates that coefficient. This is the
winner's curse, and it invalidates a naive interval whether or not the
identifier's own internal estimand was de-biased by cross-fitting (León and
Anderson 2026a). The same selection distorts the estimate for the patients
outside the subgroup.

**What is corrected, and how.** The target is the standard-analysis effect of
the selected region, with the candidate family held fixed: $\beta(\hat H)$ for
the region and $\beta(\hat H^{c})$ for its complement. Two routes remove the
optimism of selection.

- **The full bootstrap** re-runs the whole pipeline — enumerate, screen,
  select — on each resample, and corrects the observed estimate by the
  bootstrap estimate of its selection bias. It is the procedure of León et al.
  (2024). It is costly, because every replicate repeats the search.
- **Multiplier resampling** (MR) never refits. Once the candidate family and
  every candidate's effect and influence function are in hand, resampling the
  search reduces to perturbing all candidate effects jointly with one set of
  multiplier weights and re-selecting; the correction is read from the
  re-selected effects, and an infinitesimal-jackknife (IJ) interval comes from
  the same draws. León and Anderson (2026a) show the IJ interval's coverage
  under standard regularity and an explicit condition on the limiting
  competition between candidates, and that MR matches the full bootstrap on a
  fixed family.
- **Model-generated families.** For DINA and GRF the candidate family is
  proposed from a surface fitted to the outcome, so a bootstrap regenerates
  it. There MR remains valid for the same conditional target — the effect of
  the selected region given the family proposed — which the bootstrap
  reproduces only under further conditions.

**This vignette** runs the GBSG analysis of León and Anderson (2026a) for the
three identifiers — forest search (FS), DINA and GRF — at the manuscript's
settings, with the multiplier correction in full (5,000 draws) and the full
bootstrap implemented and run at a small number of replicates to show the
machinery and its cost. The manuscript's Table S2 (Supplementary Section S6),
computed with B = 1,000 bootstrap replicates, is reproduced for comparison.
`vignette("forestsearch")` runs the companion analysis of León and Anderson
(2026b) on the same trial — the search, the one-sided bounds and the
declaration calibration; this vignette is about the two-sided correction and
the bootstrap it replaces.

## The data

```{r data}
df <- survival::gbsg
df <- within(df, {
  id          <- seq_len(nrow(df))
  time_months <- rfstime / 30.4375
  grade3      <- ifelse(grade == "3", 1, 0)
})
confounders <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")
stopifnot(nrow(df) == 686, sum(df$status) == 299)
whole <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hormon, data = df)
sprintf("Whole trial: %d patients, %d events, hazard ratio %.3f (%.3f, %.3f)",
        nrow(df), sum(df$status), exp(coef(whole)), exp(confint(whole))[1],
        exp(confint(whole))[2])
```

## The settings

The analysis of León and Anderson (2026a), Section 6, and the calls below
follow the document that produced its Table S2:

- **Candidates** are conjunctions of at most two covariate cuts with at least
  60 patients and 10 events in each arm. Forest search carries ten candidate
  cuts on each receptor with zero forced in as a cut of its own; DINA and GRF
  propose their candidates from a fitted surface on the covariates as given.
- **Forest search** screens at a hazard ratio of 1.0 and requires splitting
  consistency at $p^\star = 0.90$, evaluated in closed form
  (`consistency_method = "resample"`); `stop_threshold = NULL` has every
  screened candidate evaluated.
- **The selection rule** is $\max_{\mathcal{A}} N(\varepsilon)$ at
  $\varepsilon = 0.10$: the largest admitted region whose effect is within 10%
  of the largest effect over the family. The companion vignette uses
  $\varepsilon = 0.20$ and returns a larger forest-search region (N 75); at
  $\varepsilon = 0.10$ the rule returns the 61 patients with no measured
  estrogen receptor and tumour size at most 35 mm — the effect-maximising
  region of that vignette's candidate table.
- **DINA** is re-ranked on the Cox coefficient against a floor of 0.90, with a
  two-fold cross-fit surface; **GRF** uses the frontier of its covariate grid,
  re-ranked on the Cox coefficient, at depth 2 with a doubly-robust-score
  floor of 0.
- **Multiplier resampling** at 5,000 draws, reported as the two-term corrected
  estimate with its IJ two-sided 95% interval (`ci_method = "ij"` for DINA and
  GRF). The forest-search fit asks for `ci_method = "field"` with
  `field_recovery = TRUE`: the two-term estimate and the IJ interval are the
  same under both settings, and the field adds the one-sided bounds of the
  companion vignette and the membership-recovery diagnostics used below.

## The three fits

The fits run on one core here (`parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential")`);
the bootstrap below uses up to two, the limit a CRAN check imposes. The
package's default plan is parallel.

```{r fit-fs}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_fs <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "consistency", consistency_method = "resample",
  hr.threshold = 1.00, hr.consistency = 1.00, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.10,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, field_recovery = TRUE),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
sec_fs <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r fit-dina}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_dina <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  subgroup_method = "dina", dina_select_statistic = "effect",
  dina_args = list(seed = 8316951, n_folds = 2),
  hr.threshold = 0.90, n.min = 60,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.10,
  mr_inference = TRUE, mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "ij", draws = 5000L),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
sec_dina <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r fit-grf}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_grf <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  subgroup_method = "grf", grf_selection = "frontier", grf_select_statistic = "effect",
  grf_depth = 2L, dmin.grf = 0.0, frac.tau = 0.8, n.min = 60,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.10,
  mr_inference = TRUE, mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "ij", draws = 5000L),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
sec_grf <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r selected}
fits <- list(FS = fit_fs, DINA = fit_dina, GRF = fit_grf)
secs <- c(FS = sec_fs, DINA = sec_dina, GRF = sec_grf)
for (m in names(fits)) {
  gm <- fits[[m]]$mr_inference
  cat(sprintf("%-4s %-28s N %3d   fit %5.1f s (multiplier stage %.1f s)   family %d\n",
              m, paste(fits[[m]]$sg.harm, collapse = " & "), gm$n_selected, secs[[m]],
              gm$timing_seconds, gm$n_family))
}
```

## The multiplier correction

For each identifier, `fit$mr_inference` holds the unadjusted (naive) estimate
of the selected region, the selection bias the draws estimate, and the
two-term corrected estimate with its IJ interval; `$complement` holds the same
for the patients outside the region. The family size is the number of
candidates the draws re-select over.

```{r mr-fs}
g <- fit_fs$mr_inference
cat(sprintf("Selection bias (log scale): %.3f over a family of %d candidates\n",
            g$selection_bias, g$n_family))
cat(sprintf("Region:     naive %.2f (%.2f, %.2f)  ->  corrected %.2f (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
            g$naive$est, g$naive$lower, g$naive$upper,
            g$debiased$est, g$debiased$lower, g$debiased$upper))
cc <- g$complement
cat(sprintf("Complement: naive %.2f (%.2f, %.2f)  ->  corrected %.2f (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
            cc$naive$est, cc$naive$lower, cc$naive$upper,
            cc$debiased$est, cc$debiased$lower, cc$debiased$upper))
```

The correction moves the forest-search region's estimate from an apparent
harm to a value near one, and widens the interval: the IJ interval accounts
for the selection's own variability, which a naive interval ignores. The
complement moves the other way and by much less — it is most of the trial, and
the selection barely touches it.

## The full bootstrap

`forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture()` draws a nonparametric bootstrap sample,
re-runs the identifier on it — the whole search, the screen and the selection,
with the front-end surfaces refitted for DINA and GRF — and records the
selected region's effect on the resample and on the original data. The
bias-corrected estimate is the observed estimate less the bootstrap estimate of
its selection bias, averaged over replicates (the correction of León et al.
2024); its interval uses an infinitesimal-jackknife variance of the bootstrap
mean with a finite-B correction. Multiplier resampling is not run inside the
replicates (`mr_in_replicates = FALSE`, the default), so each replicate costs
one search.

The manuscript used B = 1,000. Here B is small, to show the implementation and
its cost: the point estimates are usable as an illustration, the intervals are
not — the finite-B variance needs B in the hundreds, the package warns below
100, and at small B the variance can fall back to its uncorrected form. Read
the interval columns of the bootstrap tables below as what the machinery
produces at this B, not as results.

Replicates are independent, so the bootstrap parallelises across them:
`forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture()` dispatches them through the **future**
framework, and `parallel_args = list(plan = "multisession", workers = k)` runs
them on k processes. The document behind Table S2 ran its B = 1,000 on 11
workers. This vignette uses at most two, the limit a CRAN check imposes
(`future::availableCores()` returns what the host allows); for a real run, set
`n_workers` below to the cores you have.

```{r bootstrap}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
n_workers <- min(2L, future::availableCores())   # set to your cores for a real run
boot_plan <- if (n_workers > 1L) list(plan = "multisession", workers = n_workers) else
  list(plan = "sequential")
B <- c(FS = 25L, DINA = 25L, GRF = 10L)
boots <- list(); boot_secs <- c()
for (m in names(fits)) {
  t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
  boots[[m]] <- forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture(
    fs.est = fits[[m]], nb_boots = B[[m]], seed = 8316951L,
    mr_in_replicates = FALSE, parallel_args = boot_plan)
  boot_secs[m] <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
}
round(boot_secs, 1)
```

The package's own summaries, shown for forest search. The first is the
bootstrap table: the naive estimate beside the bootstrap-corrected one, for the
region and its complement.

```{r boot-summary}
summ_fs <- summarize_bootstrap_results(sgharm = fit_fs$sg.harm, boot_results = boots$FS,
                                       create_plots = FALSE, est.scale = "hr")
summ_fs$table
```

`mr_estimates_table()` puts the multiplier correction into the same layout: it
takes the bootstrap table as its template — the descriptive columns and the
naive estimate — and replaces the corrected column by the two-term estimate
with its IJ interval, so the two corrections can be read side by side in one
format.

```{r mr-table}
mr_estimates_table(fit_fs, boot_results = boots$FS, est.scale = "hr", digits = 2)
```

## Naive, bootstrap and multiplier side by side

The three columns for the three identifiers, assembled from the fit objects
and the bootstrap objects. The bootstrap column carries the point estimate
only: at this B its interval is not a result (the package's own table above
shows what the machinery returns for it).

```{r three-columns}
three_columns <- function(method, fit, boot) {
  g <- fit$mr_inference; cc <- g$complement
  n_H <- g$n_selected; n_Hc <- cc$n
  f2 <- function(e, l, u) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", e, l, u)
  data.frame(
    method = method, region = c("H", "Hc"),
    n = c(sprintf("%d (%d%%)", n_H, round(100 * n_H / (n_H + n_Hc))),
          sprintf("%d (%d%%)", n_Hc, round(100 * n_Hc / (n_H + n_Hc)))),
    naive = c(f2(g$naive$est, g$naive$lower, g$naive$upper),
              f2(cc$naive$est, cc$naive$lower, cc$naive$upper)),
    bootstrap = sprintf("%.2f", c(boot$H_estimates$H2, boot$Hc_estimates$H2)),
    multiplier = c(f2(g$debiased$est, g$debiased$lower, g$debiased$upper),
                   f2(cc$debiased$est, cc$debiased$lower, cc$debiased$upper)))
}
side_by_side <- rbind(three_columns("FS", fit_fs, boots$FS),
                      three_columns("DINA", fit_dina, boots$DINA),
                      three_columns("GRF", fit_grf, boots$GRF))
boot_label <- sprintf("Full bootstrap estimate (B = %d / %d / %d)",
                      B[["FS"]], B[["DINA"]], B[["GRF"]])
knitr::kable(side_by_side, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr",
             col.names = c("Method", "SG", "n (%)", "Naive", boot_label,
                           "Multiplier (5,000 draws)"),
             caption = paste("This vignette's run: hazard ratios with 95% intervals;",
                             "the bootstrap estimate at a small B, without an interval."))
```

Table S2 of León and Anderson (2026a), as published, with the full bootstrap at
B = 1,000:

```{r table-s2}
table_s2 <- data.frame(
  method = c("FS", "FS", "DINA", "DINA", "GRF", "GRF"),
  region = rep(c("H", "Hc"), 3),
  n = c("61 (9%)", "625 (91%)", "89 (13%)", "597 (87%)", "82 (12%)", "604 (88%)"),
  naive = c("2.54 (1.25, 5.17)", "0.61 (0.47, 0.79)", "1.60 (0.88, 2.91)",
            "0.63 (0.48, 0.82)", "1.95 (1.04, 3.67)", "0.61 (0.47, 0.80)"),
  bootstrap = c("1.94 (0.89, 4.21)", "0.63 (0.43, 0.93)", "0.89 (0.38, 2.07)",
                "0.66 (0.40, 1.11)", "1.04 (0.49, 2.24)", "0.66 (0.39, 1.13)"),
  multiplier = c("1.44 (0.62, 3.36)", "0.64 (0.40, 1.03)", "1.11 (0.45, 2.75)",
                 "0.66 (0.40, 1.09)", "1.05 (0.47, 2.34)", "0.66 (0.41, 1.06)"))
knitr::kable(table_s2, row.names = FALSE, align = "llrrrr",
             col.names = c("Method", "SG", "n (%)", "Naive", "Full bootstrap (B = 1,000)",
                           "Multiplier"),
             caption = "Table S2 of León and Anderson (2026a), as published.")
```

```{r reading-values}
#| echo: false
r2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
gd <- fit_dina$mr_inference; gg <- fit_grf$mr_inference
```

- **Naive and multiplier columns.** The regions, their sizes, the naive
  estimates and the multiplier estimates and intervals are those of the
  published table at its precision: the calls, the seed and the draw count are
  the manuscript's.
- **The bootstrap column** at this B is an illustration of the implementation.
  At B = 1,000 the manuscript finds the two corrections agree closely for GRF
  (1.04 and 1.05), remain apart for forest search (1.94 and 1.44, both well
  below the naive 2.54), and fall on opposite sides of one for DINA (0.89 and
  1.11) — the two routes estimate the same selection bias from different
  perturbations of the search, and DINA's family is itself regenerated by the
  bootstrap.
- **Reading, by location.** The forest-search region's corrected estimates,
  `r r2(fit_fs$mr_inference$debiased$est)` by multiplier resampling and
  1.94 by the manuscript's bootstrap, sit far below its naive
  `r r2(fit_fs$mr_inference$naive$est)`: most of the apparent harm was
  selection. The complement's corrected estimate,
  `r r2(fit_fs$mr_inference$complement$debiased$est)`, is a benefit at least as
  large as the trial's own 0.695 for the patients outside the region. Neither is
  read as a test at a hazard ratio of one.

### The cost of the two corrections

```{r cost}
cost <- data.frame(
  method = names(fits),
  mr_seconds = sapply(fits, function(f) f$mr_inference$timing_seconds),
  bootstrap_B = B[names(fits)],
  bootstrap_seconds = boot_secs[names(fits)])
cost$seconds_per_replicate <- cost$bootstrap_seconds / cost$bootstrap_B
cost$projected_B_1000 <- round(cost$seconds_per_replicate * 1000)
plan_label <- if (n_workers > 1L) sprintf("%d workers", n_workers) else "one process"
knitr::kable(cost, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Method", "MR (s)", "B", "bootstrap (s)", "s per replicate",
                           "projected at B = 1,000 (s)"),
             caption = sprintf(paste(
               "Wall-clock timings from this run: the multiplier stage under the fits'",
               "sequential plan, the bootstrap on %s. The projection is linear in B",
               "at that worker count."), plan_label))
```

The multiplier correction is seconds; the bootstrap is minutes at the B its
intervals need, and the ratio widens with B. The seconds are those of this
machine and this package version: the MR column is the whole multiplier stage
as the fit records it (`timing_seconds`); the bootstrap column is the whole
`forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture()` call on `r plan_label`, in wall-clock
seconds, so the per-replicate figure and the projection fall as workers are
added. The manuscript's figures — 72 s to about 10 minutes at B = 1,000 on 11
workers, 0.1 to 0.4 s for the multiplier stage — were recorded under
forestsearch 0.2.0 on another machine, and are not comparable second for
second; the order of magnitude between the two routes is the point.

## Diagnostics

### The re-selection frequency

$\hat p(\hat H)$ is the frequency with which the re-selection picks exactly the
identified region across the multiplier draws. It is a recorded diagnostic —
computed after the correction, read by no construction, and estimated from the
same draws — so it is a flag, not an instrument.

```{r phat}
ph  <- g$reselection$p_hat
cat(sprintf("p-hat(H) = %.3f over a family of %d candidates\n",
            unname(ph[[g$selected_label]]), g$n_family))
print(round(sort(ph, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5], 3))
```

A small $\hat p$ says the exact boundary of the region is not stable under
perturbation; by itself it is neither evidence for nor against the correction.

### What $\hat p$ alone cannot say

$\hat p$ counts exact re-selections. Over a family in which most candidates
differ from $\hat H$ by a single cut, a small exact-match rate is compatible
with the draws re-selecting near-twins of $\hat H$ or unrelated regions, and
$\hat p$ does not distinguish them. Membership agreement does: each draw's
re-selection is compared with $\hat H$ as a set of patients, in the vocabulary
of the cross-validation agreement metrics of `forestsearch_Kfold()` (`sens_H`,
`ppv_H`). These diagnostics are computed from the field draws, which the
forest-search fit asked for.

```{r recovery}
rc <- g$field$recovery
cat(sprintf("sens_H = %.3f   mean share of H retained by a re-selection\n", rc$sens_H))
cat(sprintf("ppv_H  = %.3f   mean share of a re-selection that lies in H\n", rc$ppv_H))
cat(sprintf("containment q10 / q50 / q90 = %.3f / %.3f / %.3f\n", rc$q10, rc$q50, rc$q90))
cat(sprintf("share of draws containing all of H = %.3f  (over %d draws)\n",
            rc$share_equal_1, rc$n_used))
```

Read together: the median draw retains
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rc$q50)` of the region's members,
`r if (rc$q10 == 0) "at least a tenth of the draws retain none of them" else if (100 * rc$q10 < 0.5) "a tenth of the draws retain under 1%" else sprintf("a tenth of the draws retain %.0f%% or less", 100 * rc$q10)`,
and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rc$share_equal_1)` of draws contain all of it.
Exact re-selection is rare; what moves from draw to draw is the boundary.
These diagnostics measure re-selection within the fixed candidate family under
multiplier perturbation; the bootstrap's and the cross-validation's recovery
rates (`forestsearch_bootstrap_dofuture()`, `forestsearch_Kfold()`) measure
re-discovery from resampled data with the family rebuilt, which is stronger and
costs a full re-run each time.

## Scope

The coverage result of León and Anderson (2026a) is for a fixed, enumerated
family — forest search's. DINA and GRF propose their families from the
outcomes, and a bootstrap regenerates them; for those identifiers the
multiplier correction targets the effect of the selected region conditional on
the family proposed, and the results above are empirical evaluations of how the
correction behaves on such families, not instances of the theorem. The
one-sided bounds, the two-subgroup claim and the declaration calibration that
build on this correction are the subject of León and Anderson (2026b) and of
`vignette("forestsearch")`.
